summary:
Guadeloupe stands under France's national framework: French criminal law, the anti-discrimination statute, the marriage regime and the rules on identity documents apply here as they do in the metropole. Same-sex relations were decriminalised in the Penal Code of 1791 and retained in the 1810 Code, though public morality provisions continued to be used against LGBTQ people. No legal penalty attaches to trans existence.

Legal gender recognition has followed the simplified French procedure since 1 January 2017 under a law signed on 18 November 2016. Surgery and medical diagnosis are no longer required, and the requirements for self-certification of gender and proof of medical treatment were dropped from the final bill. A change of first name can be handled at the registry office; a change of the gender marker still requires an appearance before a court. A 2017 bid to have the law recognise a 'neutral sex' classification was rejected by the Court of Cassation, and in 2022 a court of appeal ruled that a transgender woman should be regarded as the mother of a child she conceived before her sex change.

Discriminatory and violent conduct is prosecuted under the law of 31 December 2004, which made homophobic, sexist, racist and xenophobic comments criminal, with a maximum penalty of a €45,000 fine and/or 12 months' imprisonment, and amended the 1881 Freedom of the Press Law to cover injury, defamation, insult and incitement to hatred, violence or discrimination on grounds of gender, sexual orientation or disability. Christian Vanneste, a serving MP, became the first person convicted under it in January 2006, though the Court of Cassation later cancelled that conviction. A conversion therapy ban passed the Senate on 7 December 2020 and was published on 1 February 2022, carrying two years' imprisonment and/or a €30,000 fine. Reported homophobic and transphobic attacks and insults rose 36% in 2019, with police identifying around 1,870 victims against about 1,380 in 2018.

Access to gender-affirming care is constrained in practice. An ILGA-Europe report in 2022 found significant problems in that healthcare: lack of self-determination, extended waiting times and inequitable access depending on location, recommending an informed-consent model. Gender dysphoria was declassified as a mental illness by decree in 2010, though French trans organisations said nothing changed beyond the announcement; transsexualism remains listed under ALD 31 with treatment funded by the Sécurité Sociale, and gender-affirming surgery has been legal domestically since 1979. The Académie Nationale de Médecine characterised the rise in trans people seeking treatment as an 'epidemic-like phenomenon' and 'a primarily social problem' and advised extreme caution on access, without changing practice.

Trans minors are a live legislative target. In March 2024 centre-right senators commissioned a report from the Little Mermaid Observatory, a body opposed to all gender transition for minors, which called transition a 'health scandal' and transness a 'social contagion'. A bill banning medical transition under 18 passed the Senate in May 2024, opposed by the Macron government, with no further update after 23 July 2024. In late 2024 the French Society of Pediatric Endocrinology and Diabetology issued the country's first trans youth guidelines, recommending puberty blockers from Tanner stage 2. In 2022 it emerged that the president of the scientific committee of DILCRAH, France's interministerial body against racism, anti-Semitism and anti-LGBT hatred, sat on the Little Mermaid Observatory; one member resigned and the president stepped away.

Custodial settings are the documented risk area. A BuzzFeed News report of January 2018 found that in French prisons, whose rules govern detention in Guadeloupe, the placement of trans women follows the legal gender recorded on the incarceration papers, which may not correspond to the person's presentation; in practice assignment is said to weigh the individual's best interests, with individual cells or placement in more welcoming wings used where possible. The national preventive mechanism (CGLPL) issued an opinion on 25 May 2021 on the treatment of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty, finding that serious violations of fundamental rights persist across places of detention, drawing on some 40 referrals since 2010.

Practical support exists on the island. Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024, offering reception, support and orientation for people of diverse identity, sexual, bodily and gender diversities, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations; the opening was attended by the visiting national minister Aurore Bergé, who announced measures to strengthen the fight against gender-based violence and discrimination in Guadeloupe, with structures adapted for overseas territories. Community organisations including Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova partnered on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025.

In education, the national Ministry of Education launched the campaign 'Tous égaux, tous alliés' in January 2019 to tackle anti-LGBTQ bullying, providing reporting services, a helpline and guidance requirements, with 17 May as a sensitisation day. In March 2019 the Higher Education Minister announced that all higher education institutions should use transgender people's preferred names, including on student cards and exam forms.
tangentialFactors:
Historic French penalties for homosexual conduct were unequal for decades: Vichy's article 334 of 6 August 1942 (later 331) set the age of consent at 21 for homosexual relations against 15 for heterosexual relations, lowered to 18 in 1974 and equalised at 15 on 4 August 1982. The Mirguet amendment of 1960 doubled penalties for indecent exposure in homosexual activity, repealed in 1980; in March 2024 the National Assembly unanimously passed a compensation bill for men arrested under that provision before 1980, with the Senate yet to vote.

Blood donation deferrals for gay and bi men were cut to four months in April 2020 and abolished entirely on 16 March 2022.

In October 2018 President Macron denounced homophobic violence as 'unworthy of France' after a rise in attacks.

In March 2008 Education Minister Xavier Darcos announced a policy fighting all forms of discrimination including homophobia in schools as one of 15 national education priorities for 2008–2009.

In February 2019 the use of 'parent 1' and 'parent 2' on school enrolment forms caused widespread conservative outrage.

Legislation to ban medical transition for under-18s passing the Senate in May 2024 prompted large-scale protests.
localsOnly:
Community members in Guadeloupe increasingly reconcile their lives with their orientation, with activism described as advancing after sister island Martinique; organisations including Secret's Out and Amalgame Humani's are active locally.

Guadeloupe's first LGBT+ centre, the Maison des Diversités et de l'Inclusion, opened on 24 April 2024 as a historic first for the island, driven by a federation of Guadeloupean associations.

Secret's Out, Queer Gang and Lovo Nova are partnering on a year of LGBT-friendly social events across Guadeloupe in 2025, described locally as a potential 'annus mirabilis' for the island's community.

Pride has been held in Paris since 4 April 1981, reaching 500,000 participants in 2019, with events in dozens of other cities.
outOfScopeNotes:
The status of the March 2024 Senate bill banning medical transition for under-18s is unresolved: no update has been recorded after 23 July 2024, and whether it advances to a National Assembly vote is not sourced here.

Whether the 2022 ILGA-Europe findings on gender-affirming healthcare waiting times and inequitable access apply with equal severity in Guadeloupe specifically, as distinct from the metropole, is not sourced.

The CGLPL's 2021 opinion covers places of deprivation of liberty in France generally; specific findings for Guadeloupean detention facilities are not separately sourced.

Civil liberties groups including Reporters Without Borders characterised the 2004 law as a serious infringement of free speech; the practical scope of that objection in Guadeloupean enforcement is unresolved.
